newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's president may be unable to enact reforms.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's president may be unable to enact reforms.

text.p: Economists on Tuesday welcomed proposals for sweeping reforms to South Korea's outdated financial sector, but questioned whether President Kim Young-sam would have the clout to push them through parliament.

Key provisions of the proposals would increase the independence of the central Bank of Korea and greatly expand its role in determining monetary policy, mainly by curtailing the authority of the Finance Ministry.
President Kim Young-sam immediately declared his support for the reforms, which were formally presented by the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform.
"I believe the commission proposals are substantial and are on the right track," said Kim, adding the proposals dealt with "long-pending, but difficult issues".
He urged the Finance Minister to submit legislation implementing the reforms to the parliament in June.
But analysts said Kim, whose authority has waned as a corruption scandal has spread to a number of close associates and one of his sons, may not have the clout to see the measures adopted.
Lee Keunmo, head of research at ING Barings, said: "I'm wondering who will really listen when a lame-duck president orders reforms to be implemented."
Lee In-Hyung, research director at LG Economic Research Institute, said: "I doubt they will be implemented because the proposals have been prepared in haste by a lame-duck government."
The commission said central bank autonomy was needed to stabilise prices because controlling inflation could be at odds with government efforts to promote economic growth.
"First of all, the central bank should be independent and its status should be enhanced so that it can implement monetary policy neutrally," President Kim said.
Lee of ING Barings said central bank independence would result in more consistent financial policies.

The commission also proposed a unified financial watchdog board to replace the three separate bodies that currently oversee banks, securities houses and insurers. Those three watchdogs now report to the finance ministry.
The unified board should be under the direct control of the prime minister and the head of the board should have ministerial rank, the commission said.
Analysts said the commission sought to limit the finance ministry's influence over the economy.
"But most of the board's new spots will be filled with former finance ministry officials, so it won't be much different," said Lee of LG Economic Research Institute.

After much discussion, the panel decided to maintain the current four percent individual shareholding limit in banks, though it said the limit could be raised to 10 percent under certain conditions and with prior government approval.

Analysts said the conditions would effectively prevent big conglomerates, or chaebol, from owning banks, eliminating concerns about the chaebols' ever-expanding reach. But the conditions would also hinder mergers and acquisitions, they said.

"People seemed to overlook the real important issues of bank ownership," said Jwa Seung-hee, president of the Korea Institute of Economy. "We need more concrete rules to let shareholders exercise their rights in board meetings, including appointing the president and setting bank policies."

Lee Hahn-koo, president of Daewoo Economic Research Institute, said the proposed reforms would contribute to the economy. But he added a caveat: "The draft was a huge-scale programme, which needs further deep study."
